1. “soll” = it is said that (information from others)
“Sollen” in its subjective sense reports information heard from others, without the speaker vouching that it's true. Equivalent: “Man sagt, dass …” / “angeblich”.
She's said to be very rich.
He's said to have been a tram driver.
The hotel is supposed to be very good (so they say).
Watch out for the objective meaning: “Du sollst um acht kommen” = you're to come at eight (you're being asked to). The context decides.
“Wollen” in its subjective sense: the subject claims something about themselves, but the speaker doubts it. It often appears with the past infinitive.
Frau Popa claims to have seen the book.
Hotte claims never to have been late in his life.
Er muss müde sein. Er ist 26 Stunden gefahren.
Er dürfte schon in Wien sein.
“dürfte” is very common in news and commentary: “Die Preise dürften weiter steigen.” = Prices are likely to keep rising.

In Sibiu word got around quickly, more quickly than on Kastanienallee, and that was saying something. On Monday half the street knew that Andrei, the beekeeper's son, was marrying a German woman, in the old church, on Saturday. On Tuesday the whole street knew that the German woman was a baker, and there were heated discussions about whether German bakers could bake cozonac (Romanian sweet bread). On Wednesday half the neighbourhood knew that the bride's grandfather was coming from Berlin, by train, and that he was said to have been a tram driver, and a writer, both at the same time, which nobody believed. And on Thursday Frau Popa from across the road was telling anyone who would listen that she had seen this grandfather's book with her own eyes in a bookshop in Bucharest, in the window, with a photo of him on the cover.

Elena told Lena all this on Thursday afternoon, in the courtyard, under the old walnut tree, in German, which she now spoke so well that she could even translate rumours, which, she said, is the hardest form of translation. “They say you're very rich,” she said. “Your family supposedly owns a whole house in Berlin. And you apparently have a doctorate.” Lena laughed. “I have a master baker's diploma,” she said. “And the house has a leaking roof.” Elena nodded seriously. “I won't tell them that,” she said. “Here people would rather believe rumours than the truth. Rumours are more interesting.”

Lena looked at the clock. It was half past four. The train from Budapest, which Ludwig was supposed to be on, should have arrived at three. Dan had left for the station at half past two. Since then nothing had been heard. Ludwig's phone was switched off, as always, because he used it, as he said, “only for emergencies” and defined an emergency as something in which someone is bleeding. Lena had advised him from the start not to go by train. Eighty-eight years old, twenty-six hours, with changes in Vienna and Budapest. She had offered him a flight. Ludwig had refused. “I've never flown,” he had said. “I'm not starting at eighty-eight. I'll go by train. I know trains.”

At twenty to five they heard the car. Dan's old Dacia turned the corner, slowly, honked twice and stopped in front of the gate. Dan got out, with a grin Lena had never seen on him before, opened the back door and helped Ludwig out, who was stiff from the long journey but upright, in his grey suit, with his stick and his old tram driver's cap. And then the other back door opened and out of the car, with difficulty, with two sticks instead of one, in a checked jacket he had had since nineteen eighty, and with an expression as if he had just completed a journey round the world, climbed: Hotte.

“It can't be,” said Lena. “Is that supposed to be Hotte? He didn't want to come at all!” For three weeks Hotte had declared that he wasn't going to Romania, under no circumstances, that he was ninety-one, that he had never been further than the Baltic Sea and that that was, as he put it, “far enough for a Berliner”. He had said goodbye on Wednesday, on the platform at Berlin Central Station, with a handshake and the remark that Ludwig should send him a postcard “with a cow on it”. And then, as Ludwig told it later, Hotte hadn't left. He had stayed where he was until the train was due to leave. And thirty seconds before departure he had got on. Without a ticket. Without a suitcase. Just with his two sticks and his checked jacket.

“The conductor wanted to put him off the train at Frankfurt an der Oder,” Ludwig told them later that evening, at the table under the walnut tree, while Hotte sat beside him and pretended none of it had anything to do with him. “Then Hotte showed him his old BVB staff pass, from nineteen sixty-eight, and claimed he was an inspector for cross-border rail transport and on official business.” Ludwig paused. “The conductor was maybe twenty-five. He believed him. He even brought him a coffee.” Hotte shrugged. “I didn't lie,” he said. “I just didn't say which century.” Then in Vienna he had bought a ticket, with Ludwig's help, and for the whole rest of the journey, as Ludwig said, “he looked out of the window like a child, sixteen hours, and made a comment about every single cow”.

The next day Hotte was the biggest rumour in Sibiu. He was said to be a German inspector. He was said to have crossed three borders with a fake pass. He was said to have been a pilot in the war, although he had been born in nineteen forty-five. Frau Popa claimed to have heard him talking to Dan's bees, in German, and that the bees had supposedly answered him. Hotte denied nothing. He sat all Friday on the bench in front of Dan's gate, in his checked jacket, with a glass of țuică (Romanian plum brandy) that Dan refilled every two hours, and greeted everyone who walked past, in Berlin dialect. The children from the street stood around him as if around a storyteller. They didn't understand a word. But they laughed when he laughed, and by the evening three of them could say “Ick bin een Berliner”, with a perfect accent.

On Saturday at two o'clock the church was full. It was a small old church on the edge of town, white, with a green spire, where Dan and Elena had been married, and Dan's parents before them, and their parents before them. Inside it smelt of incense and beeswax, for all the candles had been dipped from Dan's wax, two hundred of them, over three evenings, by Elena and Lena together. On the walls hung old icons, darkened by the smoke of many centuries, with golden haloes that gleamed in the candlelight. In the front row, on her own chair, which Dan had carried from home to the church that morning, sat Grandma Viorica, ninety-two years old, all in black, with a white headscarf and a rosary in her hands.

Next to her sat Ludwig and Hotte. That hadn't been the plan. But on Friday evening, after Dan had told her all about the two old men from Berlin, Grandma Viorica had insisted that they sit next to her. “Whoever travels twenty-six hours by train to see a child get married,” she had said in Romanian, and Elena had translated, “sits in the front row. And whoever travels without a ticket, likewise. He needs the blessing more.” So there they sat, three old people, two hundred and seventy-one years between them, as Elif worked out later when she saw the photos: a Romanian woman who had never been to Germany and two Berliners who had never been to Romania, and none of them spoke the others' language.

The ceremony lasted an hour and twenty minutes. Ludwig didn't understand a word, but he understood everything. He saw how the priest, a big man with a grey beard, held the two crowns above the heads of Lena and Andrei, golden crowns, old and a little dented, the crowns that had been held above the heads of bridal couples in this church for a hundred and fifty years. He saw how Lena and Andrei, with the crowns on their heads and candles in their hands, were led three times around the altar, slowly, in a circle, while the choir sang, three old women and a young man, with voices that sounded as if they came from the walls themselves. And he saw how Grandma Viorica next to him was singing softly, with her eyes closed, and how her hand, without her seeming to notice, sought his.

After the ceremony, outside in front of the church, in the clear August light, when everyone was crowding round the bride and groom and throwing rice and Dan was handing out honey to everyone, whether they wanted it or not, Frau Popa came up to Ludwig. She had, as Elena explained in a whisper, a question, and had asked Elena to translate. Frau Popa looked Ludwig up and down for a long time, at the tram driver's cap, the stick, the grey suit. Then she asked: “Is it true that you're said to have been a tram driver? And a writer?” Ludwig nodded. “Both,” he said. “First one, then the other. The first for forty years. The second for barely one.” Elena translated. Frau Popa thought about it. Then she said something Elena translated with a smile: “She says: then it must be a good book. Anyone who has driven people around for forty years must have heard a lot.”

In the evening, at the party in the courtyard, under the walnut tree, with fairy lights among the branches and tables full of sarmale (stuffed cabbage rolls), mici (grilled meat rolls) and cozonac, which Lena had baked herself to disprove the rumour that German bakers couldn't, Hotte gave a speech. Nobody had asked him to. He stood up, with his two sticks, tapped his glass with a teaspoon and spoke, in Berlin dialect, for five minutes, and Andrei translated into Romanian as best he could, making up, as he admitted later, about half of it. What Hotte had really said only Ludwig found out. It was a single sentence, at the end, quietly, just for him, when Hotte sat down again: “Took me ninety-one years to figure out there's people livin' beyond the Baltic too. Thanks for not chuckin' me off the train.”

On Sunday morning, when everyone else was still asleep, Grandma Viorica took Ludwig to the workshop at the end of the garden. She didn't speak German and he didn't speak Romanian, but they didn't need language. She showed him the workbench at which her husband, Andrei's grandfather, had carved wood for fifty years, the knives still hanging on the wall, in a row, ordered by size, and a shelf on which stood a single little wooden bird, rough and clumsy, with only one wing, which her husband had carved at fourteen. “Prima” (the first), she said, and pointed at the bird. Then she pointed at Ludwig and made a movement as if she were writing. Ludwig understood. He nodded. Then he took the little bird in his hand, carefully, and gave it back to her. Viorica shook her head and closed his fingers around the bird. He was to keep it. A man who had only started writing at eighty-six should have the first bird that a boy had once begun clumsily, without knowing that fifty-two more would follow.

When Ludwig and Hotte got back on the night train to Budapest on Tuesday, both with tickets this time, standing on the platform in Sibiu were not only Dan, Elena, Lena and Andrei but also Frau Popa and the three children from the street who could say “Ick bin een Berliner” and said it very loudly as the train set off. Hotte stood at the window and waved with both sticks. Ludwig sat in the compartment, with the little wooden bird on the fold-down table. Hotte sat down opposite him when the platform had disappeared and looked out of the window for a long time, at the hills, the cows, the church spires in the distance. Then he said, without looking at Ludwig: “Know what, Ludwig? I'm gonna send myself a postcard. With a cow on it. So I still believe it next year.”
